chunks.text: Plumeria rubra, the red frangipani (commonly called champa in India and Pakistan, araliya in Sri Lanka and cempaka or kalachuchi further east), is a deciduous, small spreading tree or large shrub, usually 2-8 metres tall, with a thick, fleshy, succulent trunk, blunt grey-barked branches, and broad green leaves clustered toward the branch tips; any broken stem or leaf oozes a milky white latex that is mildly toxic and can irritate skin and mucous membranes, though it is not dangerously poisonous except in unusually large quantities. Its real fame rests on its flowers: terminal clusters of intensely fragrant, five-petalled blooms, 5-7.5 cm across, ranging from white and yellow-centred through pink to deep red depending on cultivar, that are most strongly scented in the evening and at night. This timing is not coincidental — the species practises 'deceptive pollination', producing little or no nectar reward while still luring long-tongued hawkmoths (sphinx moths) with scent alone to transfer pollen between flowers, a trick that works because the moths cannot easily tell in advance which blossoms are nectar-poor. Native to Mexico, Central America and parts of Colombia and Venezuela, where it grows in hot, dry, rocky terrain up to about 1,500 m elevation, it was carried across the Pacific by Spanish galleon trade via Manila starting in the 1560s and from there naturalised throughout tropical and subtropical Asia and the Pacific Islands, where it is now far more culturally prominent than in its native range. Hawaii in particular turned it into a major commercial crop for lei-making — over 14 million flowers were sold for leis in a single reported year (2005) — while across South and Southeast Asia it became deeply embedded in temple landscaping: it is routinely planted around Hindu and Buddhist temple grounds and graveyards alike, used as an offering placed at the feet of deity images, and in Cambodia its flowers are used to decorate coffins. Its common English name 'frangipani' traces back to the Italian Frangipani noble family and a sixteenth-century perfume associated with them, and the genus itself was named by Linnaeus for the French Franciscan botanist Charles Plumier; the species is the national flower of both Nicaragua (sacuanjoche) and Laos (dok champa), and it suffers from a distinctive fungal disease, Coleosporium plumeriae ('frangipani rust'), that coats young leaves with powdery orange-brown pustules.

chunks.source: Citizen Matters Bengaluru — "The tree that never perishes" (temple champa / frangipani culture)
chunks.text: This piece on Bengaluru's urban trees explores why frangipani/champa is so often called the 'temple tree' in Indian cities, tracing the association to the plant's remarkable physical hardiness — a broken, leafless frangipani branch stuck straight into dry ground will often root and leaf out again with no water or care for weeks, a trait that long ago got folded into its symbolism as a tree of endurance, devotion and rebirth, reinforced by its habit of flowering even on apparently dead-looking, leafless branches in the dry season. The article notes the plant's genuinely ambivalent cultural status in South Asia: the same fragrant white-and-yellow or pink blooms that are offered daily at Shiva and Devi shrines across India are, in other regional traditions (including parts of Bengali culture, where the flower is called chômpa or chãpa), associated instead with funerals, graveyards and mourning, so the symbolism of a given frangipani planting depends heavily on local and community context rather than being fixed across all of India. It also flags a genuine point of taxonomic confusion worth treating cautiously: popular and devotional writing about 'temple champa' frequently does not distinguish carefully between Plumeria rubra and the closely related Plumeria alba, and some writers cite a contested claim that a 2nd-century BCE stone relief at Mathura depicts a frangipani flower — a claim complicated by the fact that Plumeria is native to the Americas and was not introduced to South Asia until centuries after the Mathura carvings, so that particular identification is disputed rather than settled.
